entries.name: Igloo
entries.purpose: dwelling; temporary hunting and travel shelter
layout: a dome about four blocks across
tunnel is built lower than the floor so cold air pools there
blocks cut in a spiral rising and leaning inward
blueprint: layer 0: . s s .|s . . s|s . . s|. s s .
layer 1: s s s s|s . . s|s . . s|s s s s
layer 2: . s s .|s s s s|s s s s|. s s .
entries.found: singly and in seasonal camps on sea ice and tundra
entries.notes: Raised in two to three hours by one skilled builder; the sleeping platform stays well above freezing inside. Blocks are cut from wind-hardened snow; a spring igloo melts and is gone.

entries.name: Qarmaq (semi-subterranean Inuit winter house)
layout: a pit dwelling entered by an angled tunnel
household and dogs shelter under one sod roof
roof turf is cut in summer and replaced annually
entries.found: in winter village sites near coast and caribou crossings
entries.notes: The settled winter house of the Arctic: holes in old sod walls face the sea. Qarmaq settlements were abandoned as stone and sod gave way to prefabricated cabins.

entries.name: Tupiq (Inuit summer tent)
parts: door flap facing away from prevailing wind
layout: a long skin tent on two ridge-pole supports
family hearths in the centre of each bay
pitched near summer fishing and berry grounds
entries.found: in summer camps of a few families near coast and rivers
entries.notes: Not a cold-weather house: it is the warm-season half of the nomadic cycle, following fish runs and berry picking. The same poles and hides travel on sleds between camps.

entries.name: Quinzhee (snow mound shelter)
parts: trampled snow mound heaped over gear
layout: pile and trample loose snow into a dome
let it settle and sinter for a few hours
hollow from inside, leaving thick walls
entries.found: wherever snow is deep and blocks for an igloo cannot be cut
entries.notes: Unlike an igloo it needs no hard, wind-packed snow and no practised block-cutting. A collapsed quinzhee is a cave-in hazard; the door must always be marked and left unblocked.

entries.name: Icehotel (Jukkasjärvi)
layout: a single long spine with suites off it
built fresh from torn-up river ice each winter
melts away each spring and is rebuilt from scratch
entries.found: one per year in Jukkasjärvi, plus imitators worldwide
entries.notes: Demolished by the spring melt and rebuilt every November; guests sleep on ice blocks wrapped in hides at about -5 C. A standing example of a fully seasonal, disposable structure.

entries.name: Heroic-era Antarctic expedition hut
cultures: British, Norwegian and Australasian Antarctic expeditions
parts: officers and men's quarters (class-divided in Scott's hut)
layout: a single-storey rectangle built to a kit of parts
Cape Evans (Scott, 1911): about 15 x 8 m, 3 m to the eaves
Shackleton's Cape Royds hut (1908): about 15 x 7.5 m
entries.found: Ross Sea coast landing sites: Cape Evans, Hut Point, Cape Royds, Cape Adare
entries.notes: Prefabricated in England, insulated with dried seaweed, and still standing frozen in the Antarctic dry climate. The blueprint of every polar base since; treat as historic sites, not as ruins to loot.

entries.name: Log cabin
parts: notched log walls (saddle or dovetail notches)
layout: a one- or two-room rectangle
chimney at one gable end in the cold North American tradition
logs shrink and settle; door and window frames are hung loose
entries.found: singly and in forest settlements across the northern hemisphere
entries.notes: The default cold-forest dwelling of three continents. Sawn timber and nails are modern; a true log cabin needs only an axe, a saw and wedges.

entries.name: Rorbu (Lofoten fisherman's cabin)
parts: fishing gear and dried stockfish loft above
layout: a small two-storey box raised over the tide
upper floor doubles as stockfish store and drying view
herring gutters and gutting sheds alongside
entries.found: clustered in rows along the Lofoten skerries; villages of 10 to 100
entries.notes: Red-painted stilts are the postcard of northern Norway; the red paint (ketone of iron oxide) acted as a cheap wood preservative. Many are now let as holiday cabins.

entries.name: Izba (Russian log house)
entries.era: medieval to early 20th century (to now rural)
layout: a single large log room divided by the stove
stove set into a corner, its mouth opening toward the room
polati above the stove is the warmest sleeping spot in the house
entries.found: villages across the East Slavic forest belt
entries.notes: The stove is the house: it bakes bread, cooks soup, cures sick children and warms the sleeping shelf at -30 C. Early izbas were smoke huts (dymnaya izba) with no chimney; the chimney came late.

entries.name: Badstofa (Icelandic turf longhouse)
parts: long gabled sod tunnel divided into bays
layout: a row of rooms strung along a gabled tunnel of turf walls a metre thick
the sleeping platform runs the length of the badstofa
grass roof regrown every summer; from a distance the house is invisible
entries.found: singly on every settled Icelandic farm; a few preserved examples remain
entries.notes: Iceland's answer to no trees: turf walls a metre thick keep out the Atlantic wind and never need paint. The communal badstofa doubled as schoolroom in the dark winter months.

entries.name: Blackhouse (taigh-dubh)
cultures: Scottish and Irish Gaelic (Hebrides, Highlands, Donegal)
parts: double stone wall with rubble core
layout: a long low rectangle divided by a wicker screen
cattle at the down-wind end, people up-wind
no chimney; smoke escaped through a smoke hole in the thatch
entries.found: crofted townships (bailes) in the Hebrides and Highlands
entries.notes: Dual-purpose design: human body heat and cattle breath warmed the same room, and slurry was kept close to the fields. Replaced by the 'whitehouse' (roughcast + slate) after 1900.

entries.name: Norse Greenland longhouse
layout: a long sod-and-stone range dug partly into the hillside
family hall flanked by service rooms
copied from Icelandic farms of the settlement era
entries.found: ruins along the fjords of the Eastern and Western Settlements (Eriksfjord and Ameralikfjord)
entries.notes: The northernmost European farms ever worked; the Eastern Settlement was abandoned by about 1450 and the Western Settlement earlier. Ruins still show the farm layout clearly in the turf.

entries.name: Yurt (Mongolian ger)
layout: a circle 6 blocks across
door faces south toward the sun
stove in the middle; flue through the crown wheel
men's side west, women's side east, altar north
entries.found: in groups of 2-8 near water and spring pasture
entries.notes: Assembled in under an hour by practice; the wheel crown doubles as a chimney collar and skylight. Mongolia still counts a quarter of its population as ger-dwelling.

entries.name: Lavvu (Sámi tent)
entries.purpose: dwelling; moved with the reindeer herds
layout: a cone of poles covered against the wind
a low collar of sod seals the base
hearth central; smoke hole always open above the fire
entries.found: singly with reindeer herding camps; now also at festivals and tourist camps
entries.notes: Sibling of the chum and tipi; the Sámi lavvu keeps a broader base and shorter poles than the Nenets chum. Modern lavvus use canvas and are used as summer camps, not winter houses.

entries.name: Chum (Nenets conical tent)
entries.purpose: dwelling; moved with the reindeer herds
layout: a slender tall cone, steeper than the lavvu
two layers of skins in winter; outer stays, inner peels off for airing
women sit east, men west; fire between
entries.found: singly and in herding camps along seasonal migration routes
entries.notes: The archetypal Arctic cone: lighter than a dwelling of logs and warmer than any tent of canvas. Still the daily home of Nenets tundra nomads west of the Urals.

entries.name: Goahti (Sámi turf and wood hut)
parts: low wooden frame set into a pit
stone or birch hearth at the back
layout: half-buried in the ground; turf laid on a wooden skeleton
family slept on birch-branch platforms
used as winter or fishing-season house, lavvu as the mobile one
entries.found: at fixed seasonal sites: winter corrals, fishing lakes, ferry crossings
entries.notes: The stationary half of the Sámi two-house system: lavvu on the move, goahti at the base camp. Norwegian 'gamme' is the same building.

entries.name: Yaranga (Chukchi reindeer-hide tent)
entries.purpose: dwelling; moved with the reindeer herds
layout: a broad cone much squatter than a chum
outer room for work and storage; inner polov for sleeping
hide layers tightened or loosened with the weather
entries.found: in herding camps across Chukotka and the Koryak highlands
entries.notes: Widest of the conical tent family: its double-hide construction traps a dead-air layer. A full yaranga takes about thirty hides to cover, all supplied by the herd.

entries.name: Balok (Evenki sledge-mounted shelter)
entries.purpose: mobile shelter for long herd migrations
parts: ridge-pole hut mounted on a broad sleigh
layout: a closed box on runners, wider than a sledge load
dragged behind the herd train like a wagon
lived in, cooked in and slept in while moving
entries.found: on long-distance reindeer convoys in eastern Siberia
entries.notes: The only cold-climate 'house' that travels with the herd at pace rather than being dismantled and repitched. Essentially a mobile room on a sledge.

entries.name: Tipi
cultures: Plains First Nations (Lakota, Cheyenne, Blackfoot, Cree, others)
layout: a tall steep cone that lets prairie wind slip around it
door faces east, away from prevailing westerlies
hearth central; flaps angled to the wind for draw
entries.found: in traveling camps; permanent-looking clusters at gatherings and ceremonies
entries.notes: A city-sized tipi village moved with the herds and left nothing behind; archaeologists find tipi rings of cobbles. Canvas replaced hide after the bison vanished in the 1870s-80s.

entries.name: Sod house (soddy)
parts: walls of sod blocks laid like brick
layout: a low flat-roofed box rising from the plain
roof sods laid root-up so grass grows on the roof
family of four to eight in one or two rooms
blueprint: layer 0: w w w w w w w|w s . . . s w|w . . . . . w|w . . . . . w|w . . . . . w|w d . . . . w|w w w w w w w
layer 1: w w w w w w w|w . . . . . w|w . . . . . w|w . . . . . w|w . . . . . w|w w w w w w w
legend: w sod blocks, d door, s stove, . air
entries.found: singly on quarter-section homesteads; farm clusters with barn and well
entries.notes: Cost almost nothing but flat prairies made the roof leak every rain and grow grass inside; bugs were a constant complaint. Displaced by timber shipped in on new railroads within a generation.

entries.name: Earthen lodge (Mandan, Hidatsa, Arikara)
parts: dome of earth over a log frame
central earth-covered hearth with cache hole beside it
layout: a great low dome a hundred paces around
door faces east toward the morning sun
cache pit for corn under the floor
entries.found: permanent earth-lodge villages along the Missouri River and its timbered tributaries
entries.notes: The settled counterpoint to the tipi; some villages held a hundred lodges and a few thousand people. Abandoned under smallpox and US pressure in the 1800s; reconstructed lodges stand at Fort Berthold and Knife River.

entries.name: Pit house (Plateau)
cultures: Interior Salish and other Plateau peoples (Secwepemc, Syilx, Nlaka'pamux, others)
parts: pit dug two to four metres deep
roof of poles laid across the pit mouth
earth and grass over the roof
ladder stair through a roof hatch
layout: a rounded pit with a low dome of earth at ground level
one family per fire; winter villages of a dozen pits
a smoke vent and hatch ladder at the centre
entries.found: winter villages on salmon rivers; summer sites were brush shelters
entries.notes: Held heat the whole winter with less wood than any above-ground house; a single fire kept four metres of earth roof warm for months. Grass grew back on the roof each summer.

entries.name: Barabara (Alutiiq sod house)
parts: pit dug in the coastal flat
layout: one or more sod rooms sunk into the ground
kitchen and sleeping areas under heavy sod
often a cluster of barabaras around a fish-drying rack
entries.found: villages on Kodiak and the Alaska Peninsula; partially excavated at Three Saints and Old Harbor
entries.notes: Held out the Aleutian storm belt better than any above-ground house; interior heat kept the sod roof thawed while snow piled on top. The Russian name 'barabara' stuck to the building type.

entries.name: Poluzemlyanka (East Slavic semi-dugout)
parts: pit half a metre to a metre deep
log walls on the pit floor
earth and turf roof at grade
layout: a small log room sunken into the ground with only its wall-tops above grade
hearth in a corner; sleeping on earth benches
cluster of dugouts formed the first Rus' settlements
entries.found: archaeological sites across the forest and forest-steppe of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus
entries.notes: The ancestor of the izba: nine centuries of continuous East Slavic building choice. Dozens of these dugouts under one later village mark the oldest continuous settlement layers.

entries.name: Mammoth-bone dwelling (Mezhyrich type)
materials: mammoth skulls, long bones and tusks
layout: a near-circular bone ring up to 7 m across
roof of poles, hides and earth over the bone frame
four such dwellings stand in a V at Mezhyrich, Ukraine
entries.found: four dwellings at Mezhyrich and others at Mizyn and Gintsy, Ukraine
entries.notes: The oldest known dwellings built entirely of animal remains, raised on a treeless mammoth steppe where timber did not exist. Bones from at least 149 mammoths went into the Mezhyrich settlement.

entries.name: Alpine chalet
parts: broad shallow-pitched roof with wide eaves
layout: two-storey box with a broad roof against snow
hay stored above the living rooms kept stock warm into spring
balconies stacked deep along the front
entries.found: alpine valleys from Savoy to the Tyrol; villages and isolated alp huts
entries.notes: The original word meant a herdsman's hut, not a villa; grandiose 'chalet-style' villas are a 19th-century romantic export to Britain and America.

entries.name: Engadinerhaus (Engadin stone-roof house)
entries.purpose: dwelling and stable, often with attached barn
parts: flat roof of thin stone slabs
layout: a tall narrow block with a nearly flat stone-slab roof
stable and fodder downstairs, family above
end-walls painted with white sgraffito on ochre
entries.found: villages of the Engadine and Val Bregaglia: Sils, St. Moritz, Guarda
entries.notes: Slab roofs shrugged off snow load and fire; every window is small against the cold. The sgraffito facades carry inscriptions, family dates and moral mottoes.

entries.name: Gassho-zukuri farmhouse
parts: huge steep thatched gable roof at ~60 degrees
earthen-floored stable and raised living floor
layout: a long house with the gable end to the valley wind
ridge aligned along the narrow valley floor
roofs re-thatched communally every 20-30 years
entries.found: village hamlets of Shirakawa-go and Gokayama; UNESCO World Heritage since 1995
entries.notes: The 60-degree roof sheds two metres of wet snow and its shape is named for hands pressed in prayer. Wada House in Shirakawa-go is 25 x 13 m and still a home, not just a museum.

entries.name: Northwest Coast plank longhouse
entries.purpose: clan dwelling; potlatch and ceremonial space
parts: fire pit and central smoke vent
totem poles at the house front
interior sleeping platforms with carved mortuary posts
layout: a big rectangular timber hall facing the sea or river
two to four hearths down the centre, one per extended family
planks lifted off in summer for airflow
entries.found: coastal village sites from southeast Alaska to Haida Gwaii and, rebuilt, to modern museums and culture centres
entries.notes: Housed 30-50 people, sometimes a whole matrilineage, under one roof. The split-plank door and carved frontage are the fixed face of the Northwest Coast tradition.

entries.name: Cise (Ainu thatched house)
parts: central open hearth with hanging pot hook
spirit window (nusa) on the east wall
layout: a low thatched house with a deep central hearth
women sat east, men west; the east window greeted the spirits
villages (kotan) lined the lower salmon rivers
entries.found: lower salmon rivers of Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kurils
entries.notes: The cise was literally a thatched shell over a sunken floor, with the fire in the middle and no chimney; smoke seasoned the thatch. Nearly every cise was replaced by Japanese-style houses after 1869.

entries.name: Tibetan stone flat-roof house
parts: massive stone walls two stones thick
flat roof of beams, earth and gravel
layout: a square block built around a courtyard
ground floor: stores and animals; family above
roof used for drying barley, chillies and dung
entries.found: towns and monastery districts of the Tibetan plateau: Lhasa, Shigatse, Gyantse, Leh
entries.notes: Walls a metre thick and no mortar weaker than the stone; the whole plateau builds like this. Monasteries such as Sera and Drepung are the type writ a thousand times larger.

entries.name: Northeast Chinese kang house
entries.purpose: dwelling; winter heating via the kang
parts: stove at the kang's corner feeding smoke through it
layout: a low flat or gable-roofed house around a courtyard
the kang runs beneath the family's bedding and warms it all night
winter meals cooked over the same fire that heats the kang
entries.found: villages across Manchuria (Liaoning, Jilin, Heilongjiang)
entries.notes: The kang is a held-over invention of cold northern China: a brick bed flue you literally sleep on. Smoke and heat banked for hours made it the warmest affordable bed in East Asia.

entries.name: Khata (Ukrainian cottage)
layout: a single-storey rectangle, white inside and out
two rooms plus a stove kitchen
storks nest on chimneys and poles; a nest counted as luck
entries.found: villages across Ukraine and southern Russia
entries.notes: Whitewashed walls reflected the sun and hid cracks; thatch kept out the snow and fed the stove at burn-out. Almost every village house kept a stork nest and a rushnyk over the door.

entries.name: Selk'nam choza (Tierra del Fuego conical hut)
parts: windbreak wall of hides facing the sea
layout: a steep cone holding out the sleet off the Beagle Channel
family hearth in the middle; hide door to the wind-sheltered side
rebuilt quickly at each new hunting camp
entries.found: seasonal camps across Tierra del Fuego's interior
entries.notes: Hunters of guanaco in one of the windiest, wettest cold coasts on Earth; the choza was the whole architecture of the people. Selk'nam population collapsed through disease and genocide by 1930.

entries.name: Bothy (Scottish mountain shelter)
entries.purpose: unlocked refuge for walkers; former herdsman, quarry and gamekeeper hut
parts: no water or electricity by rule
fireplace or stove where one exists
layout: one open room or two small rooms
no booking, no fees, no warden
bothy code: leave it as found, take rubbish out
entries.found: remote Scottish Highlands and islands; a few in Wales, England and the Irish hills
entries.notes: A hut deliberately kept minimal: no locks, no wardens, no charges. The bothy network is the last free shelter system in Britain and a living piece of estate history.
